before.label: Thomas Kuhn
before.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms.
before.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing.

after.label: Thomas Kuhn
after.description: Explains scientific development through normal science, disciplinary commitments, crises, and revolutions. Paradigms organize problems and standards of inquiry. Later sociologists adapt these arguments, sometimes in ways Kuhn disputes; this is not a universal law that all intellectual history moves through discrete paradigms. His preface acknowledges Koyré, Metzger, Maier and Fleck as distinct resources. The later distinction between shared disciplinary commitments and exemplary solutions makes “paradigm” more precise.
after.representative_figures_and_works: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962; expanded second edition 1970). Distinguish his analysis of scientific communities from loose uses of paradigm to mean any school of historical writing. Read the 1962 preface alongside the 1969 postscript included in the second edition: sources of the argument and later clarification are different evidence.

before.label: Bruno Latour / laboratory studies
before.description: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme.
before.representative_figures_and_works: With Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life: The Social Construction of Scientific Facts (1979). The revised 1986 edition drops Social from the subtitle. Latour is one contributor within a wider field.

after.label: Bruno Latour / laboratory studies
after.description: Studies the practical work through which scientific claims become established facts, including experiments, inscriptions, instruments, and relations among researchers. Laboratory ethnography offers a route into science studies that should not be collapsed into textual interpretation or into Bloor’s programme. The Pasteur study extends his inquiry into historical scientific change and distinguishes that analysis from an explanation by social forces alone.
after.representative_figures_and_works: With Steve Woolgar, Laboratory Life: The Social Construction of Scientific Facts (1979). The revised 1986 edition drops Social from the subtitle. Latour is one contributor within a wider field. Les Microbes: guerre et paix, suivi de Irréductions (1984; translated as The Pasteurization of France, 1988) joins historical investigation to a separate theoretical argument.

before.label: Sociology of scientific knowledge / SSK
before.description: Investigates how scientific beliefs become accepted within social practices and institutions. before.representative_figures_and_works: David Bloor, Knowledge and Social Imagery (1976; second edition 1991); Barry Barnes. The symmetry principle is a rule for explanation, not a claim that all scientific assertions have equal evidential merit.
